attributes.title: The Moral Economy of Education Reform in Mexico
attributes.description:
How could public education systems be reformed in Latin America? Education reforms are a contentious issue in the region, given that influential teacher unions vehemently oppose changes in teacher hiring and promotion practices. For instance, some countries in Latin America have implemented standardized teaching evaluations, while in others, teachers' unions have successfully blocked these changes. 

This research explores several questions related to public education in Mexico using survey experiments. First, we will examine how teachers' unions shape public attitudes towards education reforms in Mexico using a vignette experiment. Second, using another vignette experiment,  we will explore whether strikes organized by teachers' unions engender public support for striking teachers or labor unions in general. Third,  we use a conjoint experiment to shed light on voters´ preferences for high-level policymakers in public education.

q2.value:
Experiment 1: Vignette about teacher evaluation

H1: Information about the benefits of teacher evaluations on learning outcomes increases support for evaluations. 

H2: Information about the benefits of teacher evaluations in reducing corruption increases support for them. 

H3: Information about teacher evaluations violating labor rights will reduce support for them.

H4: Information about teacher evaluations negatively effecting the local cultural competence of teachers will reduce support for them.

Sub-Group Hypotheses for Experiment 1

H5: Information about the positive impact of teachers' evaluations (i.e., improving learning outcomes and reducing corruption) has a stronger positive effect on support for evaluations among respondents with higher levels of education (i.e., college graduates).
 
H6: Information about the benefits of teacher evaluations in reducing corruption in the teachers' union does not increase support for respondents who live in rural areas (i.e., live in small municipalities). 

H7: Information about the benefits of teacher evaluations (i.e., on learning outcomes and in reducing corruption) does not increases support for evaluations among MORENA voters.
 
*************************************************************************

Experiment 2: Vignette on the moral economy of teacher strikes

H1: Any information about teachers striking (compared to information about teachers being unionized) decreases support for labor unions, overall. 

H2: Information about teacher labor grievances increases support for labor unions, overall and striking teachers.  

H3: Information on the private political interests of union leaders decreases support for  labor unions, overall and striking teachers.  

H4: Information about teacher labor grievances and the private political interests of union leaders decreases support for  labor unions, overall and striking teachers.  

***************************************************************************

Experiment 3: “Conjoint” evaluation of candidates to be Secretary of Education

H1. Respondents prefer lawyers and business leaders to be secretary of education compared to leaders of the teachers' union.

H2: Respondents prefer candidates that support teaching evaluations. 

H3: Respondents are indifferent about whether candidates support higher teacher salaries.

H3: Citizens prefer candidates that oppose participation of business sector in public education.

question.value:
This study employs three experiments embedded in an in-person survey in Mexico.

Experiment 1
Respondents will be presented with a randomly assigned hypothetical vignettes on the positive and negative information about the teaching evaluations. The experimental treatments are modeled after the education reforms implemented by President Enrique Peña Nieto in 2013, which established standardized teacher evaluations, and the subsequent reforms by President Andrés Manuel López Obrador in 2019, which rolled back these evaluations. 
The control condition displays descriptivie information about teaching evaluations. The first treatment condition presents information on positive effects of teaching evaluations on teacher quality and better learning outcomes. The second condition displays information on corrupt practices of teachers´ union in Mexico. The third presents information on negative effects of teacher evaluation on labor rights, while the fourth mentions that these evaluation unfavor teachers with a knowledge of the culture and customs of the local communities. 
After reading the vignette, respondents are asked whether they support or oppose the teaching evaluations (7 point Likert scale) and how likely are they sign a petition supporting teaching evaluations. 

Experiment 2
Respondents will be presented with randomly assigned hypothetical vignettes on the occurrence of teachers strike and different messages conveyed by striking teachers and their opponents (state government).
The control condition displays descriptive information about teachers being unionized. The first treatment condition gives respondents information about the teachers strike in Tamaulipas (occurred in September 2023). The second treatment presents respondents the information on strike occurrence plus teachers grievances related to pay. The third treatment presents respondents the information on strike occurrence plus information on political interests of unions leaders. The fourth treatment presents respondents the information on strike occurrence plus double framing of grievances of teachers and political interests of unions leaders.
After these randomly assigned treatments, respondents are asked do they support union influence in Mexico in general, do they support striking teachers in the state of Tamaulipas and whether they think that Secretary of Education in Tamaulipas should resign.  

Experiment 3
We use a conjoint experiment to explore voter preferences for high-level policymakers in education. We present respondents with hypothetical profiles of candidates for Education Secretary in Mexico. Respondents will evaluate two hypothetical profiles of candidates, with randomly assigned attributes in four dimensions (policy preferences in terms of standardized evaluations, teacher salaries and participation of business sector in public education and previous experience). 
The conjoint profiles include the following attributes (with different levels):

ENG attribute levels here

1. Previous experience
a. Lawyer
b. Entrepreneur
c. Leader of the teachers union (SNTE)

2. Teacher evaluation	
a. Support
b. Oppose

3. Teacher salary increase
a. Support
b. Oppose
 
4. Increasing participation of private companies in public education
a. Support
b. Oppose

q7.value: We use simple randomization for all of our experiments -- SurveyToGo randomly assigns a different treatment to each respondent.

question.value: The survey experiment will be included in the Mexico Omnibus Study, conducted by Data Opinion Publica y Mercados. This is a nationally representative sample of Mexican adults (18 years and older). Data Opinion Publica y Mercados will begin collecting responses in late October, 2023. Enumerators will ask the participants a number of questions that are part of multiple projects.

q11.value: The survey is conducted with 1000 respondents, grouped into 100 survey clusters.

question.value: Control and Treatment conditions for all experiments in English and Spanish in the attached file.

Experiment 1: Vignette about teacher evaluation

The outcome variable will be support for teacher evaluation. We will measure this by asking participants 'Do you favor or oppose the use of teacher evaluation for teachers who aspire to enter the profession?' (on a scale of 1-7, 1 being completely against and 7 being completely in favor) and 'how likely are you to sign a citizen petition in favor of teacher evaluation ?' (on a scale of 1-7, 1 being not at all likely  and 7 being very likely).

********************************************************************

Experiment 2: Vignette on the moral economy of teacher strikes

There are two outcome variables.

The first is support for labor unions, overall.We will measure this by asking participants 'Thinking about unions in general, would you personally like unions in Mexico to have more influence, the same influence, or less influence than they have today?' (1. Much more influence, 2. Some more influence, 3. The same influence, 4. A little less influence, 5. Much less influence.

The second outcome variable will be support for teachers striking. We will measure this by asking participants 'Do you support or oppose the teachers who are striking in Tamaulipas?' (on a scale of 1-7, where 1 being totally oppose and 7 means totally support) and 'Faced with the teachers' strike, do you think that the Secretary of Education of Tamaulipas, Lucía Aimé Castillo Pastor, should resign or should remain in office?' (1. You must resign, 2. she should remain in the position). 

**********************************************************************

Experiment 3: “ Conjoint ” evaluation of candidates to be Secretary of Education

The single outcome variable will be which candidate profile respondents prefer. We will measure this by asking participants "Which of these two candidates do you prefer?"

**********************************************************************

Control variables
Socio-demographic variables: Age, Gender, Education, Income
Partisanship

For the main hypotheses, we are interested in estimating the average treatment effect (ATE) across all subjects. For sub-group hypotheses, we estimate the average conditional treatment effect (CATE). We will use ordinary least squares regression (OLS) to assess the ATE and CATE for the outcome described above.

q18.value: There are no additional transformations required.

q19.value: We will use the standard p<.05 for determining if OLS suggests that the results are significantly different from 0.

q20.value:
We will verify that subjects answered each question. 

For Experiment 2: Vignette on the moral economy of teacher strikes, we will exclude respondents who were assigned to the Control condition (which did not include information about the strike) and answered the questions about support for the strike and support for the secretary of education in Tamaulipas from our statistical analysis.

q23.value:
We modeled our experiment, in part, on this article: 

Hertel-Fernandez, Alexander, Suresh Naidu, and Adam Reich. "Schooled by strikes? The effects of large-scale labor unrest on mass attitudes toward the labor movement." Perspectives on Politics 19.1 (2021): 73-91.

However, whereas Hertel-Fernandez et al found that teacher strikes in the US increase support for striking teachers and labor unions, more generally, we expect to find the opposite effect in Mexico because the political context is different and the union is perceived very differently.
